title: Essay Writing
notes: An essay is a structured piece of writing that presents the author's argument, analysis, or description on a particular topic. In the NEB Class 11 English examination, essay writing is one of the most important components, typically carrying 10-15 marks. A well-written essay has a clear introduction (opening paragraph that introduces the topic), a well-organised body (multiple paragraphs developing the main points), and a concise conclusion (closing paragraph that summarises the main ideas and leaves a final impression).

Essays are classified into four main types: Narrative essay — tells a story or recounts an event (e.g., 'My most memorable experience'). Descriptive essay — paints a picture with words, describing a person, place, or thing (e.g., 'My favourite season', 'A rainy day in Kathmandu'). Expository essay — explains or informs about a topic using facts and examples (e.g., 'The importance of education', 'How to prevent pollution'). Argumentative/Persuasive essay — presents a viewpoint and supports it with reasoning and evidence (e.g., 'Should mobile phones be banned in schools?'). NEB exams typically require expository or argumentative essays.

A good essay follows a three-part structure: (1) Introduction — begin with a hook (interesting opening sentence), provide background context, and state the thesis statement (main argument or purpose). The introduction should be 10-15% of the total length. (2) Body paragraphs — each paragraph should focus on one main idea, supported by examples, explanations, or evidence. Use topic sentences to introduce each paragraph's main point. Aim for 3-5 body paragraphs. (3) Conclusion — restate the thesis in different words, summarise the main points, and end with a final thought, recommendation, or call to action. The conclusion should be 10% of the total length.

Before writing, spend 3-5 minutes planning your essay. Jot down the main points you want to make, arrange them in logical order, and decide on a thesis statement. A simple outline helps prevent rambling and ensures coherence. For argumentative essays, consider both sides of the issue before presenting your position. For expository essays, list the key points you will explain. Good planning saves time during the actual writing and produces a more organised, coherent essay.

The introduction is the first impression your essay makes. A strong introduction: (1) Grabs attention — start with a question, statistic, quote, or vivid statement. 'Did you know that over 80% of Nepali students use smartphones daily?' (2) Provides context — give brief background information about the topic. (3) States the thesis — clearly express your main argument or purpose. Avoid starting with dictionary definitions ('According to the dictionary, pollution is...') — this is weak and clichéd. Your introduction should be 3-5 sentences for a standard essay.

Each body paragraph should follow the PEEL structure: Point (topic sentence stating the main idea), Evidence (examples, facts, or data supporting the point), Explanation (explain how the evidence supports your point), Link (connect back to the thesis or to the next paragraph). Transitions between paragraphs are essential for coherence: 'Furthermore', 'In addition', 'On the other hand', 'However', 'Consequently', 'For example'. Each body paragraph should be 80-120 words for a standard essay. Avoid including too many ideas in one paragraph — one main idea per paragraph is the golden rule.

The conclusion should not simply repeat the introduction — it should synthesise the essay's arguments and leave the reader with a lasting impression. A good conclusion: (1) Restates the thesis in new words (not copied from the introduction). (2) Summarises the main points briefly (one sentence per point). (3) Provides a final thought — a recommendation, prediction, call to action, or broader implication. Avoid introducing new information in the conclusion. For argumentative essays, end with a strong statement reinforcing your position. Keep the conclusion to 3-5 sentences.

Frequently assigned essay topics in NEB Class 11 include: 'The importance of English language learning', 'Advantages and disadvantages of mobile phones', 'Environmental pollution and its effects', 'The role of youth in nation-building', 'Benefits and drawbacks of tourism in Nepal', 'Should examinations be abolished?', 'The importance of reading newspapers', 'My favourite season', 'A memorable day in my life', 'The impact of social media on young people', 'Problems and solutions of traffic congestion in Kathmandu'. Preparing outlines for these common topics is an effective revision strategy.

Essay writing requires a formal tone — avoid contractions ('don't' → 'do not'), slang ('gonna' → 'going to'), and overly casual language. Use the third person ('one', 'people', 'students') rather than the first person ('I', 'me') in formal essays, though first person is acceptable in narrative and descriptive essays. Use transition words to connect ideas: 'however', 'therefore', 'moreover', 'consequently', 'nevertheless', 'in contrast', 'for instance'. Varied sentence structures (simple, compound, complex) make the essay more engaging. Avoid repetition of the same words — use synonyms and paraphrasing.
confusion: Expository vs. Argumentative essay: An expository essay explains or informs about a topic objectively (e.g., 'The causes of air pollution'). An argumentative essay takes a position and tries to persuade the reader (e.g., 'Air pollution control should be the government's top priority'). Expository essays present facts; argumentative essays present claims with evidence.

First person vs. Third person in essays: In formal expository and argumentative essays, use third person ('one', 'students', 'society') rather than first person ('I', 'my'). First person is acceptable in narrative and personal descriptive essays. Using 'I' in a formal argumentative essay weakens the objectivity of the writing.

Introduction vs. Background: The introduction is not just background information — it must include a thesis statement (the main argument or purpose). Background provides context; the thesis states your position. A common mistake is writing a long background without a clear thesis, leaving the reader unsure of the essay's direction.

Conclusion vs. Summary: A conclusion does more than summarise — it synthesises the essay's arguments and provides a final thought or broader implication. A summary simply repeats what was said; a conclusion adds value by connecting the points to a larger picture or suggesting action.

Contractions in formal writing: Contractions like 'don't', 'can't', 'won't', 'it's' are inappropriate in formal essay writing. Use full forms: 'do not', 'cannot', 'will not', 'it is'. This is a common error that costs marks in NEB exams.
practice: Write a thesis statement for the essay topic: 'The advantages and disadvantages of social media.' [Answer: 'While social media has transformed communication and provided unprecedented access to information, it also poses significant risks to mental health and privacy, requiring careful regulation and digital literacy.']
Write an introductory paragraph (5 sentences) for the topic: 'The importance of learning English in Nepal.' Include a hook, background, and thesis statement.

Identify the PEEL structure in this paragraph: 'Online learning has become increasingly popular. For example, many Nepali universities now offer distance education programmes. This allows students in rural areas to access quality education without relocating. Therefore, online learning promotes educational equity.' [Answer: Point = Online learning is popular; Evidence = universities offer distance education; Explanation = allows rural students access; Link = promotes educational equity]

Convert this informal sentence to formal: 'Kids these days are always glued to their phones and it's a real problem.' [Answer: 'Young people today are constantly engaged with their mobile phones, which has become a significant concern.']
Write a concluding paragraph for an essay about 'The benefits of tourism in Nepal.' Include a restated thesis, summary, and final thought.

Correct the error: 'I don't think that mobile phones should be allowed in schools because they distracts students from their studies.' [Answer: 'I do not think that mobile phones should be allowed in schools because they distract students from their studies.'] (contraction + subject-verb agreement)
Outline an essay on: 'Problems and solutions of traffic congestion in Kathmandu.' Include thesis, 3 body paragraph topics, and conclusion focus.

Write a topic sentence for a body paragraph about 'The economic benefits of tourism in Nepal.' [Answer: 'Tourism has become one of the most significant contributors to Nepal's economy, generating substantial revenue and employment opportunities.']

Identify the type of essay required for each topic: (a) 'My most memorable trip to Pokhara' (b) 'Should the NEB examination system be reformed?' (c) 'The effects of climate change on Nepali agriculture.' [Answer: (a) Narrative (b) Argumentative (c) Expository]

What is wrong with this introduction? 'Pollution is when the air, water, and soil become dirty. It is a big problem in Nepal. In this essay, I will talk about pollution.' [Answer: Weak hook (dictionary definition), no clear thesis, informal tone ('talk about'), vague and generic. A better introduction would start with a striking fact or question and state a specific argument about pollution in Nepal.]
universalFacts: The essay as a literary form was pioneered by French writer Michel de Montaigne in the 16th century. The word 'essai' means 'attempt' or 'trial' in French, reflecting Montaigne's intent to explore ideas rather than prove definitive conclusions.

In the NEB English examination, essay writing typically carries 10-15 marks out of the total written paper. A well-structured essay with clear arguments, proper organisation, and good language use can significantly boost a student's overall score.

The PEEL structure (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) is a widely taught framework in Nepali secondary schools for building effective body paragraphs. It ensures that each paragraph has a clear focus and contributes directly to the essay's thesis.

Argumentative essays in NEB exams often present a controversial topic, requiring students to take a position and support it with reasoning. Students should prepare to argue both sides of common topics, as they may be asked to present either a pro or con position.

The most common essay topics in NEB Class 11 exams revolve around education, environment, technology, and national development — themes that are directly relevant to Nepali students' lives and current affairs.

A well-written essay of 250-350 words should take approximately 30-40 minutes to compose, including 3-5 minutes of planning. Time management during the exam is crucial — students who spend too long planning may not have sufficient time to write and revise.
